articles.title: Netanyahu gets major legal boost as court casts doubt on corruption case
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s yearslong corruption trial took a significant turn in his favor on Wednesday as judges recommended that prosecutors drop charges in the most serious of the three cases against him and reconsider a second case.
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s yearslong corruption trial took a significant turn in his favor on Wednesday as judges recommended that prosecutors drop charges in the most serious of the three cases against him and reconsider a second case. In televised remarks later Wednesday, Netanyahu said the recommendations amount to a vindication and declared, “This trial needs to end immediately.” Speaking at the Israeli parliament, or Knesset, the prime minister said: “It took 10 years of terrible suffering for me, my wife and my sons for the truth to finally be revealed to everyone. Who will give us back those years, during which my sons couldn’t go out to a restaurant or walk around the city?” Netanyahu’s political allies also immediately celebrated the decision. “After years of persecution against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the time has come to put an end to a trial that was tainted from the outset, divides Israeli society, and exacts a heavy price from the country,” Defense Minister Israel Katz, a Netanyahu ally, said in a statement on X. Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman, who is presiding over the trial of Israel’s longest-serving leader, indicated to Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara in a hearing that a conviction of Netanyahu in what’s known as Case 4000 is unlikely and the case should be dropped. “It seems to us that the bribery charge presents considerable difficulties,” the court said, according to a spokesperson. “There is serious doubt as to whether the evidentiary foundation supports this allegation.” In this case, prosecutors alleged that Netanyahu gave regulatory benefits worth more than 1 billion shekels (approximately $300 million) to his friend, millionaire Shaul Elovitch, whose telecommunications company Bezeq owned the Walla! news website. Netanyahu faced a charge of bribery and another charge of fraud and breach of trust in this case. The court emphasized that its recommendations in these cases were not final decisions or a judgment in the corruption trial, but the statements alone are nevertheless an enormous win for Netanyahu. In his remarks in response to the recommendations, Netanyahu repeated Wednesday that he is prepared to form a unity government with the parliamentary opposition. Netanyahu’s political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, is maneuvering to form a government that would oust the prime minister and his far-right partners after nearly four years in power. Verdict or ‘appropriate plea agreement’ Justice Minister Yariv Levin shared one of Netanyahu’s old social media posts in which he said, “There will be nothing because there is nothing,” which became one of Netanyahu’s catchphrases when the cases began. Baharav-Miara, who does not normally attend the trial, was summoned by the court to attend Wednesday’s hearing. The attorney general said she would “carefully review” all of the court’s recommendations with the prosecution team. “There are only two ways to bring the case to a conclusion: a verdict or an appropriate plea agreement that reflects the nature of the acts and offenses,” she said during the hearing. The court also recommended reconsidering Case 2000, in which prosecutors had alleged that Netanyahu sought favorable coverage in one of Israel’s top newspapers in exchange for limiting the circulation of one of that paper’s main rivals. Netanyahu faced the charge of fraud and breach of trust in this case. “We have serious doubts as to whether the conduct described in the indictment actually constitutes a criminal offense,” the court said bluntly. In the final case, known as Case 1000, the court urged Netanyahu’s attorneys to come to an agreement with prosecutors. In this case, Netanyahu is charged with fraud and breach of trust over allegations that he received gifts such as cigars and champagne from overseas businessmen. But this case was viewed as far less serious than Case 4000, and it would be a major political victory for Netanyahu if it’s the only one left standing. The court said it seemed that Case 1000 could be “brought to a conclusion.” Netanyahu was indicted in Jerusalem District Court in January 2020. At the time of the announcement, he was in the US visiting President Donald Trump during his first term. Hours after the indictment came down, Trump unveiled what would become known as his “Deal of the Century” to solve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. The indictment made Netanyahu the first sitting Israeli prime minister to appear in court as a defendant. The criminal trial, which began in May 2020, has lasted through several wars, multiple elections and two US presidents. Netanyahu began testifying in the trials in December 2024. But the saga began earlier. Police said there was sufficient evidence to indict Netanyahu in February 2018. From the beginning, Netanyahu proclaimed his innocence, deriding the prosecution as a political witch hunt. Last December, Netanyahu formally requested a pardon. In a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, he said the trial had become “a focal point of fierce controversy” for which he bears “broad public and more responsibility, with an understanding of the overall ramifications of these events.” In the one-page letter, Netanyahu did not admit guilt or commit to anything about his political future. One month earlier, Trump wrote his own letter to Herzog asking him to grant Netanyahu a full pardon. “While I absolutely respect the independence of the Israeli Justice System, and its requirements, I believe that the ‘case’ against Bibi, who has fought alongside me for a long time, including against the very tough adversary of Israel, Iran, is a political, unjustified prosecution,” Trump wrote in the letter. In Israel, only the president has the authority to issue a pardon. Netanyahu’s main rivals, who seek to oust him after the election in late October, have yet to issue a statement following the court hearing. Max Saltman in New York contributed to this report.

articles.title: US court convicts Huawei of theft: A history of Chinese firm’s global woes
articles.summary: Chinese tech giant has faced legal problems from Europe to Asia, and its products have been banned in trade war with US.
articles.body:
A United States jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei and three of its subsidiaries guilty of serious violations, including defrauding banks and conspiracy to steal trade secrets from US firms.

The verdict on Tuesday was handed down in a New York federal court and came after a lengthy trial of the Chinese electronics and tech giant.

Huawei faced multiple allegations, including accusations of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. But the company’s troubles extend as well to a number of other countries, including Canada and Australia.

“For over two decades, Huawei built its global empire on a foundation of fraud, theft and deception,” said Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva of the Criminal Division of the US Department of Justice.

“Huawei’s crimes threatened the US financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market and undermined our national security.”

Huawei was convicted on 10 of 11 counts along with its Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co Ltd and US subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc and Huawei Device USA Inc.

The jury found them guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA and money laundering conspiracy.

In a statement, the US Justice Department revealed specific instances of alleged misconduct.

A Huawei employee stole information about Tappy, a robot developed by T-Mobile, although both firms had signed a nondisclosure agreement, the department alleged.

In another instance, Huawei engineers were accused of copying the source code of Cisco routers.

Another employee allegedly disguised as someone else went to work for the US tech company CNEX even though the firm had earlier indicated it did not want to work directly with Huawei.

The convictions also related to allegations that Huawei operated in Iran and North Korea, countries under US sanctions, and made false statements to US officials and banks to hide that fact.

Huawei, however, was acquitted of the most serious charge: engaging in criminal racketeering conspiracy.

Criminal charges were first brought against the company in 2019. Its lawyers said investigators used isolated cases of wrongdoing by a few employees to paint a grand conspiracy.

Sentencing is set for September although Huawei’s lawyers said the company will appeal.

Huawei is expected to pay huge sums in penalties.

Is this part of the US-China tech tussle?

Yes. Washington and Beijing are in a race to command technological advancements, particularly artificial intelligence.

Beijing has condemned the verdict as an attempt by Washington aimed at “containing and suppressing” Chinese firms.

“The Chinese government firmly opposes movies by the US side aimed at containing and suppressing Chinese enterprises, and firmly supports Chinese enterprises’ lawful rights,” the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on Wednesday.

The verdict was announced as the Nvidia scandal has been rocking Silicon Valley. Jensen Huang, the cofounder and CEO of the advanced chips company, is under US investigation for potentially leaking critical information to China after it was revealed a woman he had a romantic relationship with could have been a Chinese spy.

Nvidia’s chips power AI products, and Washington has restricted the company from selling its most advanced semiconductors to China. Nvidia is the world’s second most valuable company after only Apple with a market capitalisation of more than $4.4 trillion.

For years, the company has been blacklisted in the US, where it is restricted from selling equipment to telecommunications carriers without special approval because of security concerns.

Other US allies have flagged it over concerns that the company is too close to Chinese authorities:

Australia and New Zealand – joined the US in banning the firm from supplying 5G equipment and services in 2018.

Britain – banned telecom providers from buying new Huawei 5G equipment after 2020 and set a deadline of 2027 to remove all existing Huawei gear from networks.

Canada – barred Huawei from supplying equipment for 4G and 5G networks in 2022. In 2018, Canadian authorities arrested Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer and daughter of founder Ren Zhengfei. She was extradited to the US, where she faced allegations of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei’s business in Iran. Charges were later dropped, and Meng returned to China in a prisoner swap.

Europe – In 2024, major German providers like Deutsche Telekom agreed to remove Chinese-made telecom equipment from 5G networks, including those from Huawei and ZTE, another Chinese manufacturer, before a 2029 deadline. Germany is also preparing sweeping bans on Chinese mobile network equipment that essentially could bar Huawei and ZTE. Other countries – including Estonia, Denmark, France, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal, Romania and Sweden – have outright banned or restricted Huawei and other Chinese manufacturers.

Japan, Taiwan and India – have also either completely excluded or restricted the company.

articles.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade: Strong winds could ground iconic balloons
articles.summary: Strong winds and heavy rain are expected to impact celebrations across the USA, with the risk that the famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade could be impacted.
articles.body:
Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.

A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.

Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.

Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.

Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions

What is the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade?

The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.

The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during World War Two, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.

It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.

However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).

There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.

However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.

The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.

In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.

Over the last few days, a cluster of showers and thunderstorms has been swarming in the Gulf of Mexico.

That area of disturbed weather is now moving northwards, close to the east coast, and deepening into a potent area of low pressure - a Nor'easter storm, so called because it delivers strong north-easterly winds which drive into the east coast.

The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for New York City, as well as Long Island and north-east New Jersey.

It comes into force part-way through the parade and warns of strong to damaging wind gusts, which could affect trees and power lines and bring significant travel disruption.

The winds are forecast to strengthen through the day peaking during the evening, meaning the very strongest gusts are likely to hit after the parade is over. However, there is a risk that they could approach the threshold that would ground the balloons.

Up to 3in (75mm) of rain could fall with the risk of flooding, which could be exacerbated along the coast as high tides arrive on Thursday evening.

Large waves and high sea levels are expected, bringing the threat of erosion and damage along the shoreline.

Other eastern parts of the USA will also receive heavy rain and strong winds, with snow in some inland parts adding to the Thanksgiving travel headaches.

articles.body: A 13-year-old from Taiwan led the design of an app that maps cigarette-butt pollution, while leading a youth group that has removed more than 30,000 discarded butts. Hao-Han “Hank” Wu began the initiative in August 2023 with five friends, forming a group called No Butts Squad 4.0. The project expanded to include teams in Taiwan and Canada. In 2024, the group became the No Butts Alliance.According to Action For Nature, the alliance has carried out more than 94 street clean-ups before they could reach the ocean. The team uses its Butt Hunter app to map plastic pollution hotspots and improve the efficiency of its clean-up efforts. Wu is upgrading the platform to Butt Hunter 2.0 by integrating AI image recognition, GIS mapping, and an open API to help municipalities track pollution trends more effectively.How does the Butt Hunter app help track cigarette-butt pollutionThe Butt Hunter app maps areas where cigarette-butt litter is concentrated. Wu and the alliance use the collected information to identify hotspots and plan clean-ups more efficiently. The group has completed more than 94 street clean-ups, removing over 30,000 cigarette butts before they could reach the ocean.Wu is now upgrading the platform to Butt Hunter 2.0. The planned version will bring together artificial intelligence image recognition, geographic information system mapping, and an open application programming interface. These tools are intended to help municipalities follow pollution trends.What tools has Wu designed to tackle cigarette-butt pollutionThe initiative began in August 2023, when Wu formed No Butts Squad 4.0 with five friends. As the project developed, it gained teams in Taiwan and Canada. In 2024, the group took the name No Butts Alliance. Its work extends beyond street clean-ups and digital mapping. Wu designed a Smart Drain Interceptor, a gutter net fitted with sensors to catch litter before it enters waterways.He also designed the Rapid Butt Picker, a walking stick presented at the International Exhibition for Young Inventors. Both projects focus on cigarette litter and its movement into the environment. The alliance has since established chapters in Canada and Japan and worked with Dutch NGO No Plastic Filter to address plastic cigarette-filter pollution worldwide.Wu takes cigarette-pollution campaign to Taiwan's policymakersWu has also taken the campaign into public policy discussions. He stood alongside Taiwan’s Vice President at the launch of the National Ocean Policy White Paper and has spoken with legislators about stronger plastic-reduction measures. In 2025 and 2026, he organised the first and second Children’s Action Forums to give young people a platform in environmental decision-making.Two weeks before the 2026 forum, its venue manager cancelled the booking, saying cigarette pollution was too negative a subject for a youth-led initiative. Wu reorganised the team and secured a larger venue. The event went ahead after cancellation with 300 participants, including Taiwan’s Environment Minister and a member of parliament. The Minister then committed to an official Children's Climate Action Forum at the Presidential Office.How did an Arctic expedition shape Wu's understanding of plastic pollutionWu’s environmental work has also taken him beyond Taiwan. He was selected for a Public Television Service (PTS) scientific expedition to the Arctic, where he spent three weeks with polar researchers studying microplastics in ice cores. The experience showed him how litter from local areas can travel through ocean systems to remote parts of the planet.He is a National Youth Representative for Taiwan’s Ministry of Education and a 2026 HundrED Youth Ambassador. He is also one of 30 recipients of the Taishin Outstanding Volunteer Award. Alongside his environmental work, Wu is a Scout leader and a multiple-time karate gold medallist. He plans to study environmental policy and sustainable governance abroad before returning to Taiwan to help protect its coastlines long-term.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Mass. turkey farm shut down by health officials days before Thanksgiving
articles.summary: A Massachusetts turkey farm has been shut down by local health officials just days before Thanksgiving.
articles.body: A Massachusetts turkey farm has been shut down by local health officials just days before Thanksgiving. The Belwing Turkey Farm in Seekonk posted about the closure on its Facebook page on Tuesday. “We have very bad news, the Seekonk board of health has shut us down in our 82nd year and we will not be able to sell turkeys Tuesday and Wednesday for the 2026 Thanksgiving season,” the announcement reads. According to a notice posted to the farm’s front window by the Seekonk Board of Health, inspectors on the property Monday determined there was an “imminent health hazard” that required an immediate suspension of business. The letter stated that the farm had been issued a food permit to allow the sale of prepackaged turkeys, specifically for Thanksgiving. However, inspectors said they found issues with compliance, including packaging discarded in the dumpsters and turkeys that had previously undergone inspection were apparently repackaged not to standard. According to the notice, the health department agent observed the following violations: Multiple tables observed in-between use in a condition not suitable for food contact.Person in charge unable to demonstrate knowledge / many priority item violations observed.No certified food protection manager on site.Observed excessive number of flies in shed used for turkey processing. The farm has said they are contacting customers to warn them about the shutdown. The business declined to comment when asked by NBC affiliate WJAR-TV.

articles.title: An Alabama landowner fighting a power company's plan to run transmission lines across his property has positioned two semi-truck trailers across an access route, escalating a legal dispute over land rights and construction
articles.summary: A landowner in Alabama has parked two semi-truck trailers at the entrance to his property to prevent Alabama Power from accessing the land, escalating a
articles.body: A landowner in Alabama has parked two semi-truck trailers at the entrance to his property to prevent Alabama Power from accessing the land, escalating a dispute over the utility company's plan to build a transmission line across his property using eminent domain.Fenn Church, who owns more than 400 acres in Shelby County, has opposed the proposed route, arguing that the power company should not be allowed to use his property's entrance and surroundings for transmission infrastructure. The dispute has reached the Alabama Supreme Court, where Alabama Power is challenging a judge's decision to reject its request for a temporary restraining order against Church.The case has also drawn the attention of influential groups, including the Business Council of Alabama and the Alabama Department of Transportation (ALDOT), which have been allowed to support the utility company's appeal through legal filings.Why Alabama Power wants access to the propertyThe dispute began after Alabama Power sought an easement to install a transmission line across Church's land. The company says it offered compensation for the access easements and right of way covering less than nine acres of his property.In a statement released earlier this month, Alabama Power said Church had been awarded $425,435 for the easements, clarifying that the payment was not for ownership of the land.The company argued that the transmission line was necessary to provide reliable electricity to its three million customers, including homes, hospitals, schools and businesses.Church, however, has maintained that he is not opposed to transmission lines or the need to supply electricity to data centres. He objects to the proposed route, saying it would bring infrastructure too close to his home and affect the privacy of his property."I'm not anti-Alabama Power. I think we got to have transmission lines. We've got to have data centers, but don't build them in people's backyards and expect to use their front driveway as your easements," Church said.Alabama agency backs power company's appealAlabama Power's legal challenge has received support from the Business Council of Alabama and ALDOT. Both groups have been granted permission to submit amicus briefs, also known as "friend of the court" filings, in the appeal.ALDOT is concerned that a ruling restricting the right of entry onto disputed land could affect how government agencies carry out future road and bridge projects. The agency argues that such a decision could make it harder for authorities to access land before property disputes are fully resolved.According to the Alabama Appellate Court, ALDOT sought additional time to submit its brief, which is due on November 30.Governor Kay Ivey's position draws Church's criticismAlabama Governor Kay Ivey's office has defended ALDOT's involvement, saying the agency must sometimes use eminent domain as a last resort to complete necessary road and bridge projects.The governor's office said ALDOT follows the law, ensures property owners receive fair compensation and treats them fairly.Church said he was "extremely disappointed" by the governor's position. He claimed he had supported Ivey throughout her political career and had invited her to visit his property to examine an alternative route.He argued that another route would be more economical and environmentally friendly, and said he was not trying to stop the transmission line from being built.Church has also questioned ALDOT's involvement in the case, claiming it presents a conflict of interest because he pays annual vehicle registration fees for his trucking business, which help fund the department.The legal dispute continues as Alabama Power seeks to overturn the lower court's decision and secure access to Church's property.You use AI every day. articles.title: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, wrongfully deported from US, arrives in Spain
articles.summary: The Salvadoran national’s lawyer said in a statement that it was ‘a temporary departure’.
articles.body:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national whose wrongful deportation to El ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Salvador drew sharp criticism of United States President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, has arrived in Spain.

Abrego Garcia did not speak to reporters as he arrived at Madrid’s main international airport on Wednesday, but raised a fist as he climbed into a van.

He voluntarily departed the US a day earlier after months of legal opposition to a second deportation, this time to one of various African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials. A judge had told him to self-deport by Tuesday, The Associated Press news agency reported, citing a source familiar with the matter.

In a post on X, the DHS said: “It’s not surprising this criminal illegal alien would choose to go to Spain, a country that earlier this year was invaded by tens of thousands of illegal aliens … Good riddance.”

Abrego Garcia’s lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, described the move as “a temporary departure”.

“Mr Abrego Garcia has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration,” he said in a statement.

Sandoval-Moshenberg noted the US government had sought to deport Garcia “in shackles on an ICE Air flight to Liberia”.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, the state where Abrego Garcia ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠lived with his family for around a decade before being deported, said the Trump administration “was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will.”

The departure of Abrego Garcia, 31, brings an end to a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Supreme Court.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Abrego Garcia in Baltimore in March 2025. He was then transferred to a megaprison in El Salvador despite a prior court order barring him from being sent to the country because of the risk of persecution.

A US official later called the transfer an “administrative error”.

After the Supreme Court ordered the government to facilitate Garcia’s return, prosecutors secured a criminal indictment charging him with human smuggling in a case stemming from an earlier incident. The Trump administration then brought him back ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠to the US in June 2025. It later tried to deport him to Liberia ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠after a US judge dismissed the human smuggling charge.

articles.title: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.summary: Young Britons are having half as much sex as they were in 1990, according to a new study, with the average reported frequency falling from four times a month to just twice a month.
articles.body: Young Britons are having half as much sex as they were in 1990, according to a new study, with the average reported frequency falling from four times a month to just twice a month. The data was produced as part of a long-running study known as the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), according to a statement Wednesday from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), which participates in the research. “The sex lives of people in Britain have changed markedly since 1990 and they have substantial and varied sexual and reproductive health needs,” LSHTM said. Researchers randomly selected around 6,700 people from England, Scotland and Wales aged 16-59 to participate in interviews and online surveys between September 2022 and January 2024. This is the fourth edition of “one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world,” which has previously been undertaken in 1990, 2000 and 2010. In addition to adults under 45 years old reporting that they are having sex half as much as their peers did in 1990, the survey showed that 77% of 16-59-year-olds reported having sex in the past year, and 89% said they had sex at least once in their lives. Among 16-24-year-olds, one in three said they had never had sex, up from around one in five in 2010. Half of young women reported watching pornography in the past 12 months, compared with nearly 90% of male respondents. This was the first time the survey had asked about the use of online pornography. Attitudes toward children and contraception are also changing. While the use of hormonal contraception declined among young women, the proportion of women who report that they don’t want children has doubled in the past decade. Rise in risky behaviors The survey also reveals important findings for preventing the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with more than one in four sexually experienced 16-24-year-olds with exclusively opposite-sex partners reporting behaviors that are associated with STI risk. These include “having four or more partners or condomless sex with two or more partners in the past year or overlapping partners in the past five years,” the statement said. “While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” Soazig Clifton, academic director for Natsal at University College London, which also participates in the survey, said in the statement. “There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many.” Dr Otilia Mårdh, a scientific officer at the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), who was not involved in the research, said that “another notable Natsal-4 finding is, that the proportion of men reporting both same-sex and opposite-sex partners (MSWM) more than doubled, from 0.9% (Natsal-3) to 2.3%.” “The authors note that this growing population could increasingly bridge sexual networks with different STI risks,” Mårdh said in a comment published by the Science Media Centre on Wednesday. She added that this is “particularly relevant” as surveillance data from European monitoring programs shows “recent increases in syphilis and gonorrhoea among heterosexual populations, alongside rising congenital syphilis — contrasting with historically lower levels.” “These trends highlight the need for accessible, stigma-free sexual health services offering prevention and testing tailored to people’s needs,” said Mårdh. Five papers drawing on the results of the survey were published in the journal The Lancet.

articles.title: Christians increasingly targeted across Europe as watchdog warns of rising hostility
articles.summary: Anti-Christian hate crimes in Europe rose 44% last year, says the Vienna observatory, which documented 2,465 incidents in 2025 across the continent.
articles.body: Attacks targeting Christians across Europe rose 44% last year, according to a new report from the Vienna-based Observatory on Intolerance and Discrimination Against Christians in Europe (OIDAC). Their research documented 2,465 anti-Christian hate crimes and incidents in 2025, with France, England and Wales, Germany and Austria recording the highest totals. "Our primary concern with the new data is that anti-Christian attacks that target persons, individuals themselves, have risen," OIDAC executive director Anja Tang told Fox News Digital. "Clergy and people responsible for places of worship were those who were most attacked and also where numbers increased most strongly." CHRISTIAN WOMAN PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO NEW 'ORWELLIAN' CHARGES FOR STANDING AND SILENT PRAYER She added, "These would be people who were present, were visible, recognizable as Christians and kind of associated with a church." Tang noted that while OIDAC’s numbers are "quite conservative," saying "aggression against individuals is highly underreported" across Europe. The group said French authorities recorded a 70% increase in attacks on individuals, the highest in Europe, although Tang notes the French government has not yet published a detailed explanation of the increase. OIDAC argues the increase in attacks against individuals warrants separate attention from incidents involving vandalism, theft and arson targeting religious property. The findings come as the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) has begun highlighting anti-Christian hate crimes through a dedicated practical guide, and amid debate over whether attacks on Christians receive the same public attention as incidents targeting other religious communities. Tang said OIDAC is one of the largest contributors of anti-Christian hate-crime data to the OSCE's reporting system, and OIDAC uses the OSCE’s methodology when classifying incidents. WORLD-FAMOUS CATHOLIC SHRINE TORCHED, 'DEVIL IN A SKIRT' SCRAWLED ON VIRGIN MARY STATUE The findings have also drawn concern from Alessandro Calcagno, deputy general secretary of the Commission of the Bishops’ Conferences of the EU (COMECE) and advisor on fundamental rights and freedom of religion within the EU. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Calcagno says "the vital and courageous work constantly carried out by" OIDAC "underscores the importance of EU mechanisms to counter a phenomenon that does exist in Europe and that therefore cannot be ignored at the institutional and policy level." Lorenzo Vidino, director of the Program on Extremism at George Washington University, says anti-Christian incidents appear to stem from a mix of sources, including anti-religious activists, some individuals from Muslim backgrounds and ordinary vandalism. Vidino said anti-Christian attacks often receive less public attention than similar incidents involving other faith groups. "There's no question there's been acts of violence against Muslims, against Jews and that's despicable. And when it happens, it is prosecuted," he tells Fox News Digital. "When the same act happens against churches or Christian sites, it doesn't happen in the same way." STATE DEPARTMENT PRESSES EGYPT TO RESPECT RELIGIOUS FREEDOM AS CHRISTIAN CONVERT FACES POSSIBLE EXECUTION "While the law might be neutral, the common perception of things is not neutral, and so those incidents are not prioritized," he said. Calcagno says protecting places of worship "cannot be reduced to acts of terrorism, but should also cover other types of attacks against them," including vandalism, violence, profanation, disruptions of religious services, arson and harassment. Tang said OIDAC is also concerned about migrant communities, including Christians fleeing persecution in the Middle East and asylum seekers "who have left Islam behind and are really facing quite severe aggression because of their choice of religion." She notes these groups "really need protection," and that most incidents involving these groups go unreported "out of fear of stigmatization." Tang said she was surprised by the number of attacks "connected to pro-life convictions" and carried out by "left-wing extremist groups" that OIDAC categorized as anti-Christian incidents in German-speaking Europe, noting "the level of this violence was just significantly more than what I have seen in my time observing these trends." CARRYING A BIBLE IN NORTHERN IRELAND HOSPITALS COULD BE A CRIME UNDER ABORTION BUFFER ZONE LAWS She pointed to a café run by a Leipzig, Germany, church that was forced to close its doors after being vandalized over 26 times because of "their Christian worldview," and an Austrian church that was forced to evacuate in the middle of holy Mass due to "a fake bomb being placed there by left-wing groups… because it was a prayer connected to a pro-life event." She said,"I find it shocking the level of violence that's often shown by groups who disagree, who plead for tolerance, but then themselves behave the most intolerant." Calcagno backs OIDAC's call for a dedicated EU coordinator on combating anti-Christian hatred, a position COMECE has repeatedly requested and one it "hopes that the European Commission will take up in the near future." He stressed that such a role would complement existing EU coordinators addressing antisemitism and anti-Muslim hatred, positions that he said "rightly exist at the EU level." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP OIDAC is urging European governments to adopt recommendations contained in the OSCE's recent practical guide on anti-Christian hate crimes, including improving the recording of incidents, strengthening prevention efforts and expanding support for victims. The group also renewed its call for the EU to appoint a coordinator dedicated to combating anti-Christian hatred.

articles.title: British woman, whose husband drugged and raped her for decades, testifies in mass sexual assault trial
articles.summary: A British woman who believed she was in a “loving” and “normal” relationship with her husband told police officers they were mistaken when initially confronted with allegations that he was drugging and raping her – and inviting other men to participate in the abuse.
articles.body: A British woman who believed she was in a “loving” and “normal” relationship with her husband told police they were mistaken when initially confronted with allegations that he was drugging and raping her – and inviting other men to participate in the abuse. In video evidence filmed shortly after her husband’s arrest, and shown to a court on Wednesday, the woman told officers, “I still can’t believe it’s true and I think you have made a mistake.” The woman’s husband, who initially denied the abuse, has since pleaded guilty to more than 60 offenses, including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration, sexual assault, administering substances with intent to stupefy or overpower, and sharing intimate imagery. Nine men are now on trial in Manchester, northern England. Seven are accused of participating in the sexual abuse of the woman at the couple’s home; two are on trial for “non-contact offenses,” accused of encouraging the abuse online. Eight deny all the charges against them, while a ninth has admitted three offenses but denies a further charge. The husband is not being named to protect the wife’s identity. Prosecutors said the husband “lived a double life masked in respectability,” while sexually abusing his wife for more than 20 years. At first, they said, he took advantage of her when she had drunk enough to put herself in a deep sleep before later using a “cocktail of stupefying drugs,” to ensure she would not wake up during the abuse. But from 2023, the husband began inviting other men to their home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, where prosecutors say they sexually abused her. The husband shared footage and photos of this with other men online “who enjoyed the fact that the (victim) was asleep or unconscious, entirely unaware of what was being done to her,” prosecutors said. In the video evidence shown in court, the woman viewed pictures of the alleged offenders and was asked if she knew them or had consented to any sexual activity with them. She repeatedly answered “no.” Facing her alleged abusers from the witness box, the woman rejected suggestions that the sex was consensual, or that she was a willing participant in a game or role-play. “That’s not true,” she said. Sleeping medication Earlier in the trial, prosecutors said the husband had extensively searched for information about prescription drugs and the dangers of mixing them with alcohol. When he was arrested, pipettes with a medicine used to treat sleeping problems were found in the couple’s bedroom. The court heard that, at certain doses, the mixture of drugs and alcohol could have been lethal. The husband’s search history also included queries about so-called date rape drugs, the court heard, as well as erectile dysfunction. In her evidence, the wife said that she had only been taking medicine prescribed to her by a doctor, including drugs for high blood pressure and cholesterol. In one of her first conversations with police, the woman described what she thought was a normal family life. “We did things together, went out with other people, we’ve always had quite a lot of friends and a good social circle,” she said. In a second police video shown in court, police showed the victim images of the men they said had been invited to sexually abuse her at their home. She was asked if she recognized or had ever spoken to any of the men. She answered “no” to all. The husband is expected to give evidence later this week. Many of the defendants met the husband on the swinging website Fabswingers before continuing their correspondence on other messaging apps, the court heard. The husband wrote on his Fabswingers profile that he was wanting to “try new and varied things.” “Married guy. Wife is hot and cold these days so will rarely be joining me,” he wrote, according to prosecutors. The husband also looked for men on fabguys.com, writing on his profile page there: “Not much experience with guys. Like showing off my wife pics to other men.” More men plead guilty Ahead of the trial, three other men scheduled to appear in court pleaded guilty to offences against the woman. They include former youth football coach Karl Lindsay, 56, who pleaded guilty to non-contact offenses of conspiracy to rape and conspiracy to administer and substance with intent. He has also admitted three separate offenses – which came to light following his arrest – of making indecent images of children. Sean Peers, 38, of Stockport, pleaded guilty to assault by penetration and Graham Brougham, 74, of Cheshire, pleaded guilty to rape. And on Monday, Robert Stewart, 70, pleaded guilty to two counts of rape, and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent. He denied a fourth charge of conspiracy to rape. Meanwhile, Keith Fotheringham, 59, of Dundee, Scotland, was the first man to plead guilty in relation to offenses against the woman at an earlier hearing in February and has not stood trial. He admitted conspiracy to rape, conspiracy to assault by penetration and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent. He also admitted one count of assault by penetration. The jury last week heard that Fotheringham sent tablets hidden in a signed Sting CD cover to the husband to drug his wife. Another man, 59-year-old Tommy Golden, also pleaded guilty this week of sexually assaulting the same woman in June 2025. He was identified and charged later than the other men and is not part of the Manchester trial. CNN’s Saskya Vandoorne contributed reporting.

articles.title: Tech billionaire plans 1,000-year floating city at sea
articles.summary: Palmer Luckey says SLAB, his floating industrial city, would last 1,000 years, hosting metal processing and oil refining beyond California rules.
articles.body: How frustrated would you have to be with government red tape to decide the ocean looks like a better place to build a factory? Tech billionaire Palmer Luckey has an answer. He wants to create a massive floating industrial city where American companies could operate beyond certain state and local restrictions. The project is called SLAB, and Luckey says it would have a design life of 1,000 years. That's a pretty extraordinary promise for something sitting in the middle of the ocean. However, the reasoning behind the project may be even more surprising than the structure itself. We discussed Luckey's ambitious plans in detail on "The CyberGuy Report Podcast" at cyberguy.com/podcast. So, what exactly is he planning to build, and could moving American industry offshore really solve the problems he's trying to escape? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. CEO SAYS DOING BUSINESS IN STATE ‘SUCKS’ AS COMPANY HEADS TO TEXAS AMID CALIFORNIA EXODUS What is Palmer Luckey's 1,000-year floating city? Palmer Luckey, the founder of Oculus and co-founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, has revealed plans for a floating industrial platform called SLAB. In a November 18 post on X, Luckey explained that he began developing the project after Facebook acquired Oculus in 2014. He used some of the money from that sale to pursue an idea that has fascinated technology entrepreneurs for years. The concept is known as seasteading. It involves building permanent structures on the ocean where people can live or operate businesses outside some of the restrictions that apply on land. Luckey's version focuses heavily on American industry. He wants to create a place where companies could conduct activities that face significant regulatory hurdles on the mainland. The illustration accompanying his announcement shows an enormous platform rising above the ocean with buildings and industrial facilities on top. AMERICA'S REDDEST STATE CHASES BILLION-DOLLAR BOOM AS OTHERS SOUR ON MASSIVE EMERGING INDUSTRY Why Palmer Luckey wants to move American industry offshore Luckey believes government regulations have made it unnecessarily difficult for certain industries to operate in the United States. His proposed solution is to move some of those operations offshore. He specifically mentioned metal processing and oil refining. He also identified desalination and medical research as possible activities for SLAB. In his announcement, Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen American industry by creating a "relief valve for ill-considered or outdated rules and regulations." His argument is that companies could operate more efficiently if they avoided certain state and local restrictions. He also wants the offshore platform to be cheaper than building comparable facilities on land, although he has not publicly demonstrated that the economics would work. There is also a more controversial possibility. In a separate exchange on X, Luckey suggested that offshore facilities could provide access to medical treatments currently prohibited in the United States. That raises difficult questions about patient safety and whether those activities could legally take place offshore. How much money is behind SLAB? Luckey says he and several close friends funded SLAB at a $1 billion valuation back in 2017. However, that figure refers to the project's reported valuation at the time. It does not establish that $1 billion has been spent building it. He also says the project has made significant progress, although considerable work remains. So far, he has not publicly disclosed a confirmed construction schedule or a precise location for the proposed platform. Interestingly, Luckey only decided to discuss SLAB publicly after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He pushed back on that description, saying the project was much older and considerably more ambitious. His comments suggest that data centers could be part of the broader concept, but SLAB was conceived for other industrial activities as well. Can a floating city really escape U.S. regulations? This is where Luckey's proposal runs into some complicated legal questions. According to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, most coastal states, including California, have jurisdiction over submerged lands extending approximately three nautical miles offshore. Beyond that boundary, federal authority becomes especially important. The United States has a territorial sea extending 12 nautical miles from its coastal baselines. It also maintains an exclusive economic zone extending up to 200 nautical miles offshore. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration explains that the federal government retains authority over certain offshore structures and activities within that zone. Consequently, moving a business beyond California's coastal boundary would not automatically eliminate federal oversight. Environmental requirements and maritime regulations could still apply. The legal picture would also depend on whether SLAB floats freely, anchors to the ocean floor or operates under a particular country's registration. Luckey has yet to explain exactly how the platform would navigate those requirements. Could an ocean city really last 1,000 years? Building a permanent industrial community offshore presents extraordinary engineering challenges. Saltwater gradually corrodes exposed structures, and powerful storms can place enormous stress on offshore installations. Maintaining a facility for centuries would require substantial engineering and ongoing repairs. Then there is the expense of running an industrial operation at sea. Workers would need transportation to the platform, while supplies and equipment would have to travel across the water. That makes Luckey's goal of operating more cheaply than comparable land-based facilities particularly ambitious. A 1,000-year design life is also a target rather than a demonstrated lifespan. Until Luckey releases detailed engineering evidence, there is no way to independently verify whether SLAB could meet that goal. Why this floating city could send a message to California California has long been associated with technological innovation, yet it also has extensive environmental and land-use regulations. Some businesses argue that permitting requirements make industrial development more expensive and time-consuming. Luckey's proposal brings that debate into focus. Moving industrial activity offshore would be a drastic response to regulatory frustration. However, the idea also raises a question worth asking: Have some regulations become so burdensome that entrepreneurs would rather build at sea than navigate the approval process on land? Of course, industries involving hazardous chemicals or experimental medical treatments require serious oversight. Those protections help prevent accidents and protect public health. At the same time, regulations can become unnecessarily complicated or outdated. Governments need to examine whether their approval processes encourage responsible innovation or create obstacles that serve little practical purpose. Luckey has not identified the specific California laws he hopes to avoid. For now, his project highlights a broader argument about how America regulates industrial development. Whether SLAB becomes a functioning offshore community remains to be seen. Kurt's key takeaways I find the whole idea fascinating, but something about it also strikes me as completely absurd. Have we really reached a point where building a giant industrial platform in the ocean sounds more appealing than dealing with government regulations on land? California, in particular, should be paying attention. This is a state that helped create Silicon Valley, yet we're now talking about taking American industry offshore to escape regulatory headaches. I'm certainly not suggesting we eliminate important environmental or safety protections. But there's a point where excessive regulation can start working against the very innovation we should be encouraging. I'd much rather see American businesses building here, creating jobs and developing new technology without unnecessary roadblocks. Luckey still has a tremendous amount to prove before SLAB becomes reality. But the fact that he's seriously pursuing this idea should give policymakers something to think about. articles.title: Yemen’s Houthi rebels attack Saudi Arabia’s largest oil refinery
articles.summary: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom’s largest.
articles.body: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels said on Wednesday they had attacked Saudi Arabia’s ⁠Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom’s largest, which sits alongside one of the world’s largest crude export terminals. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the refinery attack caused fires. Satellite imagery from both NASA and Planet Labs showed thick black smoke over the installation. A source with knowledge of the matter confirmed an attack on the ⁠refinery, which covers about 230 square miles or roughly ​the ⁠size of Chicago. The Saudi government and state oil firm Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Houthi militia, which controls much of western Yemen including the ⁠capital Sanaa, has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s ​frozen civil ⁠war reignited in July in a ‌spillover from the U.S.-Iran war. The attacks have previously temporarily disrupted some of Aramco’s operations and caused the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh. They also forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or ‌cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup and ‌flagship investment conference FII. The Saudi-led coalition said earlier on Wednesday that air defenses had intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. It did not say the refinery there had been struck. Ras Tanura, which has ⁠a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, has previously been hit during the conflict with the Houthis as well as during the broader Iran war. It is part of a complex on the kingdom’s Gulf coast that was the kingdom’s main export terminal until the U.S.-Iran war boosted the importance of Yanbu on the west coast, which receives oil via the East-West pipeline. The Houthi spokesperson Saree had also said the group attacked Riyadh’s financial district ‌in three phases. Saudi civil defense said 11 people were wounded on Tuesday in a ​strike on a tower in Riyadh’s financial district, the tallest building in the ‌capital that houses the headquarters of the Public ⁠Investment Fund, the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. It was the second strike on the ⁠tower in less than a week. The first, on Nov. 19, damaged the building but caused no injuries. The Saudi ‌civil defense posted an image ​on Tuesday of the landmark tower showing some ‌damage to the building about halfway up the ​facade, similar to the impact from last week’s attack.

articles.title: Iraq’s top court rules government can take over Kurdish borders, oil fields
articles.summary: The ruling comes a day after Kurdish authorities accused Baghdad of an ‘assault’ on the region’s constitutional rights.
articles.body:
Iraq’s top court has ruled that the federal government can deploy troops to the country’s international borders, including in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.

Wednesday’s ruling comes a day after Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal forces to take over Kurdish-run border crossings and demanded authority over oil fields controlled by Kurdish security forces, in an effort to curb oil smuggling.

Kurdish authorities denounced the move, with the regional government calling it “an assault” on the region’s “constitutional rights”.

The Federal ⁠⁠⁠⁠Supreme Court also ruled that federal authorities could oversee agencies operating at all border crossings, including those in northern Iraq’s Kurdish region, though they must coordinate with regional and provincial governments on customs administration, state television reported.

The court said the federal oil ministry can also oversee and audit oil and gas fields, while Baghdad shares responsibility for managing the oil and gas they produce with regional governments and producing provinces, according to state TV.

The Iraqi government did not specify how or when the takeover would be implemented.

The move comes just a week after al-Zaidi also took on Kataib Hezbollah – a powerful Shia militia aligned with Iran – following oil smuggling allegations.

He ordered troops to prepare to enter the city of Jurf al-Sakhar, a Kataib stronghold south of Baghdad. The group initially responded with defiance but allowed soldiers into the city, following a compromise brokered by Shia politicians.

The court’s decision appears to be a victory for al-Zaidi, but analysts say it will be challenging to implement moves against the Kurds and the heavily armed Shia militias loyal to Iran.

Renad Mansour, deputy director of the Middle East and ‌‌‌‌North Africa programme and director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said Iraq’s judiciary was “very much supportive” of the government’s campaign to establish a centralised political order.

“The Iraqi government [is] trying to reclaim some sovereignty … because it’s such a fragmented state where there isn’t a centre,” he said.

A senior Shia politician close to Zaidi told the Reuters news agency that the prime minister was trying to dismantle the model of a “state within a state”. He added that al-Zaidi was trying to restrain armed factions operating above state authority, as well as draw clearer limits on the semi-autonomous Kurdish region’s exercise of authority over strategic economic and security matters.

The Kurdistan Regional Government on Wednesday rejected what it called “military ⁠⁠⁠⁠language and threats” in a statement from the Iraqi military announcing the new measures. It said ⁠⁠⁠⁠it was working with federal authorities to combat corruption and called for an end to oil smuggling across Iraq.

Iraq’s state news agency, citing what it said was a federal government intelligence report, said oil belonging to the state-owned North Oil Company was being diverted and smuggled from Kirkuk, as well as from Sulaimaniyah inside Iraq’s Kurdish region, to Iran and onward to Afghanistan.

Also on Wednesday, the Syrian and Iraqi defence ministers discussed “several issues of mutual interest” over the phone, according to Syria’s Ministry of Defence.

articles.title: A 16-year-old girl was found murdered after leaving work in Ontario in 1968; 58 years later, preserved DNA has identified former firefighter Michael Joseph Moore as the suspect, but he died before he could face charges
articles.summary: After 58 years, DNA evidence has identified Michael Joseph Moore as the suspect in the 1968 murder of 16-year-old Jacqueline Dunleavy in Ontario, Canada, but he passed away in 2018 before he could face charges.
articles.body: Police in Ontario, Canada, have identified a former firefighter as the man responsible for murdering a 16-year-old girl nearly 58 years ago, after modern DNA testing helped solve a case that remained unresolved for decades. Investigators named Michael Joseph Moore, who died in 2018, as the suspect in the killing of teenager Jacqueline 'Jackie' Dunleavy.Dunleavy was found dead on January 9, 1968, after finishing her shift at a convenience store in London, Ontario. According to the London Police service, preserved biological evidence from the original investigation was re-examined using modern forensic technology and genetic genealogy, eventually leading investigators to Moore.He was 25 at the time of the murder but died on March 3, 2018, before police identified him. Consequently, no criminal charges can be filed against him.The breakthrough was announced at a police news conference on Monday. Chief Thai Truong said the outcome reflected the work of investigators across generations and the importance of preserving evidence for future forensic examination.Who was Jackie Dunleavy and what happened in 1968?Dunleavy was a Grade 10 student at Westminster Secondary School and the daughter of a London police officer. She also worked at Stanley Variety Store on Stanley Street, near Wharncliffe Road.On January 9, 1968, she finished her shift at approximately 6.30 pm and left the store on foot. Police believe she was heading towards a bus stop to catch a ride home, as she regularly did.Around 8 pm, three young people discovered her body on the grounds of Katherine Harley School, now the location of Matthews Hall, on Oxford Street.Investigators determined that she had been strangled. She had also suffered a head injury, while contemporary news reports noted that a pink tissue box had been placed in her mouth.Police interviewed witnesses, followed several leads and collected biological material from the scene. However, the investigation failed to identify the person responsible, leaving the case unsolved for decades.Witnesses recalled seeing a girl matching Dunleavy's description waiting at a bus stop on Beaconsfield Avenue before entering a white vehicle. Police also received information about an earlier incident in December 1967, when Dunleavy reportedly accepted a lift from a man who had recently arrived in Canada and spoke with an English accent.Detective Mike Budzyn said the girl had apparently missed her bus after work. However, he stressed that investigators had no direct evidence establishing that the man described by the witness was Moore.DNA evidence helped to solve the murderThe investigation gained momentum decades later as forensic technology made it possible to examine evidence that could not be fully analysed in 1968.Dunleavy's murder was among the cases reviewed under Project Angel, a joint initiative involving the London Police Service and Ontario Provincial Police that operated between 1997 and 2001.Moore's name emerged during that earlier review, but he was not identified as a suspect or person of interest. Records from that investigation have since been lost, according to Detective Sergeant Micah Bourdeau.In the latest review, investigators sent preserved evidence to Othram Laboratories in Texas, which specialises in forensic investigative genetic genealogy.The technique uses DNA information and genealogical research to identify distant relatives and establish family connections that can help narrow down potential suspects.According to London police, specialised testing identified distant genetic relatives connected to the unknown DNA profile. Investigators then worked with the Toronto Police Service to build family trees and identify a potential suspect.Further interviews were conducted, and new forensic samples were collected for comparison. These were submitted to the Centre of Forensic Sciences, which helped confirm Moore's DNA match.Budzyn said the evidence had reached the threshold required to support criminal charges."Had Moore been alive today, he would have been arrested and charged in relation to Jackie's murder," he said.Who was Michael Joseph Moore?Moore was born in Ireland in 1942 and moved to Canada in January 1967, according to police. He settled in London, Ontario, and moved into an apartment on Springbank Drive in May that year.He was 25 when Dunleavy was killed. Police described him as white, approximately six feet tall, with dark hair. He was generally clean-shaven but sometimes grew a beard while on holiday.Moore later worked as a firefighter in Ireland and London, eventually reaching the rank of captain. An obituary published in the London Free Press stated that he spent 28 years in the profession.He was not working as a firefighter when the murder occurred. Moore retired from the London Fire Department in 2002 and died on March 3, 2018, following a long illness. He was survived by his wife and three children.London Fire Chief Lori Hamer said the announcement had affected members of the department and offered condolences to Dunleavy's family."While we cannot speak to the actions of the former employee, today's news has been deeply troubling for many within the London Fire Department," Hamer said.Police have also stated that there is no evidence Moore and Dunleavy knew each other.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Minnesota dam built in 1910 to generate electricity survived decades of floods before suffering severe damage in 2024; more than $21 million in federal funding has now been approved for its removal
articles.summary: The Rapidan Dam in Minnesota is an enduring structure that has survived years of flooding and damage.
articles.body: The Rapidan Dam in Minnesota is an enduring structure that has survived years of flooding and damage. However, it suffered major structural damage during the destructive flooding events of the summer of 2024. After years of standing strong, the dam is now set to be removed.Blue Earth County has received approval for more than $21 million in funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to move ahead with the removal of the Rapidan Dam, as reported by KEYC News on November 23, 2026. The county is in the process of finalising details, including the design and planning stages, with demolition expected to begin in 2027, provided all permits are approved. The project will also involve restoring the riverbanks affected by the 2024 flooding.A dam that once powered the regionLocated on the Blue Earth River in Rapidan Township, approximately 12 miles south of Mankato, the Rapidan Dam has been part of Minnesota's landscape for well over a century. According to Blue Earth County's official records, the structure was built between 1908 and 1910 to generate hydroelectric power for the Mankato area. It was constructed using hollow reinforced concrete, with a height of approximately 87 feet from the top of the dam to the riverbed and a length of 475 feet.The dam was initially an important part of the region's electricity infrastructure. In fact, when it first began operating, it helped double the power-generating capacity of Mankato's electric system.However, the structure's relationship with the river was never particularly straightforward. Flooding was not an unusual event for the dam, and the 1965 flood caused severe damage to the structure, bringing electricity generation to a halt.Northern States Power Company, which owned the dam, eventually transferred ownership to Blue Earth County in 1970. It was only after a period of extensive repairs and modifications to the dam's powerhouse that hydroelectric power generation resumed in 1984.Years of flooding and repairsThe Rapidan Dam's history is closely tied to repeated attempts to maintain it against the changing conditions of the Blue Earth River. According to Blue Earth County's historical account, emergency repairs were required in 2002 after significant erosion had affected the dam's foundation. Further repair and maintenance work followed in 2010 and 2017, particularly involving the dam's foundation, concrete structures and protective apron.The situation became increasingly difficult following severe flooding in 2019 and 2020. The 2019 event damaged the dam's steel gates, training wall and apron, affecting its ability to function normally. Flooding and ice-related damage in 2020 also affected the powerhouse, eventually bringing electricity generation at the facility to a halt. The dam has remained out of service as a power-generating facility since then.The county had already begun examining what could be done about the ageing structure. In 2021, it commissioned two feasibility studies, one considering the possibility of repairing the dam and another examining its removal.What happened during the 2024 floods?The most infamous chapter in the dam's history unfolded in June 2024, when heavy rainfall across southern Minnesota caused the Blue Earth River to rise dramatically. According to Blue Earth County's environmental assessment documentation, the watershed received approximately eight to nine inches of rainfall over three days, from June 22 to June 24, 2024, causing extreme runoff conditions.As the river exceeded the dam's capacity, a large accumulation of debris also became lodged near its gates, making an already difficult situation more challenging. The water eventually eroded the western side of the dam, cutting a new channel around its west abutment rather than simply passing through the existing spillway.The damage to the dam was incredibly severe, as the river began carving through the surrounding western valley wall. Within approximately three days, the river had shifted more than 300 feet from its earlier alignment, according to the county's environmental assessment documentation. The flooding also led to the loss of the upstream reservoir, Rapidan Lake, as water escaped through the newly formed channel.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Massachusetts man won $1 million lottery prize, posed for a photo with oversized check; ICE tracked him down, claimed he had a deportation order since 2014
articles.summary: A Salvadoran national who won a $1 million prize in the Massachusetts State Lottery was arrested by federal immigration officers just six days after
articles.body: A Salvadoran national who won a $1 million prize in the Massachusetts State Lottery was arrested by federal immigration officers just six days after collecting his winnings, following a brief foot chase in East Boston. Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales was taken into custody by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers early Tuesday, November 24, according to three federal immigration sources cited by Fox News. The 25-year-old reportedly tried to flee on foot when officers approached him but was quickly apprehended. Multiple officers' body cameras recorded the arrest, the sources said.The arrest came less than a week after the Massachusetts State Lottery awarded him a $1 million prize on November 18. The lottery had posted a photograph of Velasquez-Morales holding an oversized ceremonial cheque on its Facebook page on November 21.According to ICE sources, Velasquez-Morales had been wanted by immigration authorities under a final deportation order issued in April 2014. He had allegedly crossed into the United States illegally near Roma, Texas, in 2013.ICE Boston confirmed the arrest in a November 25 social media statement, saying Velasquez-Morales entered the US illegally on May 15, 2013, and was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014.How he won the $1 million lottery prizeThe Massachusetts State Lottery said Velasquez-Morales purchased the winning $10 scratch-off ticket, called "$2,000,000 50X Cashword", at a market in East Boston. He was awarded the $1 million prize on November 18. Three days later, the lottery shared his photograph holding the oversized cheque, announcing his win. The same East Boston neighbourhood where he purchased the winning ticket was where ICE officers subsequently arrested him. It is unclear what will happen to the lottery winnings following his arrest or whether the federal immigration proceedings will affect his ability to retain the prize.Can undocumented immigrants buy lottery tickets in Massachusetts?Massachusetts lottery rules allow anyone aged 18 or older to purchase tickets from authorized retailers. The rules do not require buyers to be US citizens or demonstrate legal immigration status to participate. The Massachusetts State Lottery is overseen by a five-member commission, with two members appointed by the governor.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ecuador and US review joint military operations, official says
articles.summary: Joint military efforts have been paused as the US investigates a lethal operation carried out by Ecuador.
articles.body:
The United States and Ecuador have held talks on reviewing operations in the South American country, which the US paused pending an investigation into one carried out by Ecuadoran forces.

That operation is believed to have been linked to a campaign against drug trafficking and illegal mining and has raised questions over whether the Ecuadoran military committed human rights abuses.

Ecuador’s interior minister, John Reimberg, said on Wednesday that last week’s talks between US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Ecuadoran President Daniel Noboa in Quito, Ecuador, were ‌‌productive and resulted in Ecuador having an “established action plan” with the US.

“Some would like to see these relationships, which have yielded so many positive results, damaged,” Reimberg said in a radio interview.

The pause in joint operations was prompted by concerns over possible crimes ‌or human-rights violations committed by Ecuadoran forces during an operation on September 23 that killed Carlos German Munoz Jara, who officials say was a high-ranking gang member, The New York Times reported.

In March, Noboa announced joint operations with the US and other allies, describing the effort as “a new phase” in the ‌fight against ‌drug trafficking and illegal mining.

Later, the Taura Air Base in Ecuador reportedly witnessed an unusual deployment of US soldiers and aircraft.

Noboa said US personnel were at the airbase solely for “temporary activities” as part of cooperation between the two countries .

He denied the US has a military base in his country.

“We work together. It’s not an American base,” he said.

Noboa has adopted hardline anti-gang policies. Under his administration, Ecuador has been constructing mega-prisons as it attempts to deal with a wave of drug violence.

The first facility, which opened in November 2025, was modelled on El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT) and has the capacity for 800 prisoners.

articles.title: NYC ICE chief attacks Mamdani, Hochul over Chinatown woman's murder, blames sanctuary policies
articles.summary: New York City's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) chief has accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul of having “blood on their
articles.body: New York City's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) chief has accused Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Governor Kathy Hochul of having “blood on their hands” over the alleged rape and murder of a 62-year-old woman in Chinatown, blaming the city's sanctuary policies for allowing the accused killer, an undocumented immigrant, to remain free despite repeated attempts to detain him.Kenneth Genalo, who heads ICE's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) in New York City, made the allegations during an interview with Fox News' Fox & Friends on Wednesday. His remarks came after it emerged that Alexander Florentino-Maldonado, a 25-year-old Honduran national, had been arrested 38 times in New York City since February 2025 but was repeatedly released despite ICE detention requests, the New York Post reported.Florentino-Maldonado is accused of sexually assaulting and strangling Jin Yu, 62, inside her Chinatown apartment on Saturday. He was reportedly released from custody just a day before the alleged killing.“This person should be alive now,” Genalo said, referring to Yu.ICE says five detention requests were ignoredGenalo alleged that ICE had issued five detainers against Florentino-Maldonado over the past year, but none was honoured by the New York Police Department (NYPD).Questioning the city's sanctuary policies, he said an NYPD spokesperson had recently claimed that the department had not honoured an ICE detainer in 10 years.“How many people have been hurt, harmed, or even killed because of that inane policy?” Genalo asked.He also rejected claims by Mamdani and Hochul that their policies were aimed at keeping New Yorkers safe.“Nothing could be further from the truth,” he said, accusing Democratic leaders of prioritising politics over public safety.“All these crimes are preventable,” Genalo added, arguing that authorities were treating undocumented immigrants differently from US citizens.ICE chief targets bail reformGenalo also criticised New York's bail reform laws, claiming they allowed repeat offenders such as Florentino-Maldonado to move in and out of the jail system so quickly that authorities struggled to keep track of them.He further accused city officials of withholding complete information from federal immigration authorities, including dates of birth, and alleged that district attorneys were being encouraged to reduce criminal charges.According to law enforcement sources cited by the New York Post, Florentino-Maldonado first entered the US illegally from Mexico in March 2022. He was apprehended by Border Patrol agents in Arizona and deported, but later allegedly re-entered the country.Between February 2025 and November 21, 2026, he was arrested 38 times in New York City and released each time, the report said.The alleged attack on Yu has renewed the debate over New York City's sanctuary policies and cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.Genalo said city and state leaders would be responsible if people were harmed after ICE detention requests were ignored.Representatives for Mamdani and Hochul did not immediately respond to requests for comment.You use AI every day.
